Sum of infinitely many terms added one after another. The terms may be numbers, functions, matrices, or anything else that can be added, written a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + ⋯. Series, also called infinite series, are a major part of [[Calculus|calculus]] and [[Mathematical analysis|mathematical analysis]]. They are used in most areas of mathematics, including combinatorics through generating functions, and in physics, computer science, statistics, and finance.

An infinite sequence of additions cannot be performed in finite time, so a value is assigned through a limit. The finite sums of the first n terms are called partial sums. If their limit exists as n tends to infinity, the series is convergent, or summable, and the limit is its sum; otherwise it is divergent. The same notation denotes both the process of adding and, for a convergent series, its result. [[Taylor series]] approximate smooth functions by polynomials with infinitely many terms.

Among the Ancient Greeks, the idea that a potentially infinite summation could produce a finite result was considered paradoxical, most famously in [[Zeno's paradoxes]]. [[Archimedes]] and other Greek mathematicians nonetheless applied infinite series, for instance in the quadrature of the parabola. The concept of a limit resolved the mathematical side of Zeno's paradoxes during the 17th century, especially through the early calculus of [[Isaac Newton]]. In the 19th century [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]], [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy]], and others made the resolution rigorous, using the completeness of the real numbers and the notions of absolute and conditional convergence.

Intangible act or use for which a consumer, company, or [[Government|government]] is willing to pay. Examples include work done by barbers, doctors, [[Lawyer|lawyers]], accountants, [[Mechanic|mechanics]], [[Bank|banks]], and [[Insurance|insurance]] companies. Public services are those that a society as a whole pays for, such as hospitals, elementary [[School|schools]], or libraries. Unlike [[Goods|goods]], which involve the transfer of tangible products, services give value to the customer through the provider's effort rather than ownership of an object.

Services are usually described by four characteristics. They are intangible: they are not manufactured, transported, or stocked, and cannot be stored for future use. They are inseparable, being produced and consumed simultaneously, so the consumer is part of the delivery. They are perishable: resources assigned to a period go unused if no one consumes the service then, as with an empty airline seat after departure. They are variable, or heterogeneous: each delivery differs in time, place, circumstances, or resources, and many services are modified for each consumer.

These traits make quality hard to keep consistent, since many services depend on variable human activity rather than a precisely determined process, and demand varies by season, time of day, and business cycle. Exceptions include utilities. A service can be specified through standard attributes, such as the benefits to the consumer, the delivery point, the times at which it is available, a fulfillment target, a delivery duration, and a price.

Services have become the dominant sector in modern economies, accounting for approximately 67% of global GDP and over 50% of employment worldwide, with higher shares in developed nations. Services often show slower productivity growth than goods, a point linked to debates such as Baumol's cost disease.

Collection of distinct things, called elements or members, typically mathematical objects such as numbers, symbols, points in space, lines, other geometric shapes, variables, functions, or other sets. Sets cannot be mathematically defined, since they form a primitive notion and are instead characterized by axioms. Since the first half of the 20th century, all mathematical objects have ultimately been defined in terms of sets, so [[Set theory|set theory]] serves as the foundation of mathematics.

Before the end of the 19th century, sets were not studied specifically and were not clearly distinguished from sequences. Most mathematicians treated infinity as potential, the result of an endless process, and were reluctant to consider infinite sets. The study of infinite sets began with [[Georg Cantor]]. It produced counterintuitive results: the number line has strictly more elements than there are [[Natural number|natural numbers]]. Assuming a set of all sets led to [[Russell's paradox]], which triggered a foundational crisis in mathematics. One resolution, [[Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory]], has been generally adopted as a foundation. [[David Hilbert]] prophesied the wide use of sets in mathematics, saying: "No one will drive us from the paradise that Cantor created for us."

A set may be specified by listing its elements or by giving a property that characterizes them. Roster notation, introduced by Ernst Zermelo in 1908, lists elements between braces, and a set does not change if elements are repeated or reordered. By the axiom of extensionality, two sets are equal if and only if they have the same elements, so only one [[Empty set|empty set]] exists. A set is finite if its elements can be put in one-to-one correspondence with the first n natural numbers, and infinite otherwise.

Prejudice or discrimination based on one's sex or gender. Sexism can affect anyone but primarily affects women and girls. It has been linked to [[Gender|gender]] roles and [[Stereotype|stereotypes]] and may include the belief that one sex or gender is intrinsically superior to another. Extreme sexism may foster [[Sexual harassment]], [[Rape|rape]], and other forms of sexual violence. It may arise from social or cultural customs and norms.

Definitions differ by field. Peter Glick and Susan Fiske coined the term ambivalent sexism for stereotypes that can be both hostile and benevolent. The feminist author bell hooks defines it as a system of oppression that disadvantages women, and philosopher Kate Manne sees it as the branch of a patriarchal order that makes patriarchal arrangements seem natural or inevitable. Functionalist sociologists such as [[Talcott Parsons]] understood gender inequality as the natural outcome of a dimorphic model of gender.

According to legal scholar Fred R. Shapiro, the term was most likely coined on November 18, 1965, by Pauline M. Leet at Franklin and Marshall College. The [[Oxford English Dictionary]] cites a print appearance in 1866. Historical examples include written laws barring women from the political process in ancient Rome,. Some scholars suggest sexism and [[Misogyny|misogyny]] helped fuel the witch trials of the 15th to 18th centuries.

Some commentators stress that men also face sexism, citing legal biases, social expectations, and [[Conscription|conscription]]. Whether disparities such as earnings gaps mainly reflect discrimination, or occupational choice and hours worked, is disputed.

Intimate social activity, typically the insertion of the erect penis into the vagina followed by thrusting motions, for erotic pleasure, biological reproduction, or both. This type is also called vaginal intercourse, or coitus, from the [[Latin]] *coitio* or *coire*, "a coming together". Other penetrative forms include [[Anal sex|anal sex]], [[Oral sex|oral sex]], fingering, and penetration with a dildo or vibrator.

Views differ on what counts as sexual intercourse. The term, especially coitus, generally denotes penile–vaginal penetration, but commonly also covers penetrative oral and anal sex, and statutory law often uses "sexual penetration". Non-penetrative sex is sometimes called outercourse, though some people or definitions count it as intercourse. The [[World Health Organization]] notes that non-English languages and cultures use different words for sexual activity with slightly different meanings. Researchers commonly use the term for penile–vaginal intercourse and specific terms for other acts.

Sexual activity carries a risk of [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infections]], and health professionals recommend safer sex practices. Jurisdictions restrict certain acts, such as adultery, incest, sexual activity with minors, prostitution, rape, zoophilia, sodomy, premarital sex, and extramarital sex. [[Religion|Religious]] views vary widely between and within religions, though a common theme is the prohibition of adultery.

Between non-human animals the term copulation is more usual, and sperm may be introduced in non-vaginal ways, such as by cloacal copulation. Most non-human mammals mate at estrus, the most fertile period of the female cycle. [[Bonobo|Bonobos]], dolphins, and [[Chimpanzee|chimpanzees]] have sex regardless of estrus and with same-sex partners, behavior presumed to be for pleasure and to strengthen social bonds.

Enduring personal pattern of romantic or sexual attraction to persons of the opposite sex or gender, the same sex or gender, or more than one gender. Patterns are generally categorized as [[Heterosexuality|heterosexuality]], [[Homosexuality|homosexuality]], and [[Bisexuality|bisexuality]]. [[Asexuality|Asexuality]], experiencing no sexual attraction to others, is sometimes identified as a fourth category, though there is significant debate over whether it is a sexual orientation.

Orientation is distinguished from sexual identity, a person's conception of themselves, and from behavior, the sexual acts actually performed. According to the American Psychological Association, it is also distinct from biological sex, gender identity, and social gender role. The term "sexual preference" largely overlaps with it but may suggest voluntary choice, whereas orientation is not a choice.

No single theory of cause has gained widespread support, but scientists favor biological theories, and the evidence for nonsocial causes is considerably stronger than for social ones, especially for males. A major hypothesis implicates the prenatal environment, specifically the organizational effects of hormones on the fetal brain. There is no substantive evidence that parenting or early childhood experiences play a role. Heritability estimates of 30–50% have been reported, and longitudinal studies show some fluidity, particularly in women, with 10–20% of individuals reporting shifts over time. Across cultures most people are heterosexual; in Western nations surveys find 90–95% of adults predominantly heterosexual, about 2–4% homosexual, and 1–3% bisexual.

The subject is studied primarily within biology, [[Anthropology|anthropology]], and [[Psychology|psychology]], including sexology, and also within [[Sociology|sociology]], history, and law.

Infection spread by sexual activity, especially vaginal intercourse, anal sex, oral sex, or sometimes manual sex; also called sexually transmitted disease (STD) or venereal disease. The term "infection" is generally preferred because it includes cases without symptomatic disease. Many STIs cause no initial symptoms, which creates a risk of transmission. Symptoms may include vaginal or penile discharge, genital ulcers, and pelvic pain, and some STIs can cause [[Infertility|infertility]].

Bacterial STIs include [[Chlamydia|chlamydia]], [[Gonorrhea|gonorrhea]], and [[Syphilis|syphilis]]. Viral STIs include genital warts, genital [[Herpes|herpes]], hepatitis B, human papillomavirus (HPV), and [[HIV/AIDS]]. Parasitic STIs include trichomoniasis, scabies, and pubic lice, and a fungal ringworm strain is an emerging infection. Most bacterial and parasitic STIs are treatable and curable with antibiotics, although gonorrhea faces growing antimicrobial resistance. Viral infections such as HIV and genital herpes are not curable but can be managed. HPV and hepatitis B can be prevented by [[Vaccination|vaccination]]. Using [[Condom|condoms]], having fewer sexual partners, mutual monogamy, and comprehensive sex education also reduce risk.

Diagnostic tests are usually easily available in the developed world but often not in the developing world. In 2015, STIs excluding HIV caused 108,000 deaths worldwide, and about 1.1 billion people had STIs other than HIV/AIDS. About 500 million had syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, or trichomoniasis, at least 530 million had genital herpes, and 290 million women had HPV. Documentation of STIs dates back to at least the Ebers Papyrus (c. 1550 BC).

Spiritual practice in which a practitioner, the shaman, interacts with the spirit world through altered states of consciousness such as trance. The usual goal is to direct spirits or spiritual energies into the physical world for healing, divination, or other help to people.

The word derives from Russian *shaman*, which comes from a Tungusic term, possibly from the Evenki or Manchu language. It is sometimes connected to a Tungus root meaning "to know", a link the linguist Juha Janhunen questions. Mircea Eliade suggested the [[Sanskrit]] *śramaṇa*, a wandering monastic figure whose word spread across Central Asia with [[Buddhism]], as a possible ultimate origin. Russians adopted the term from the Indigenous peoples of [[Siberia]]. Nicolaes Witsen carried it to Western Europe in his book *Noord en Oost Tataryen* (1692), and a 1698 account of a Russian embassy to China by Adam Brand introduced it to English speakers.

Anthropologists have no single agreed definition. Manvir Singh proposes three basic features: entering non-ordinary states, engaging with unseen realities, and providing services such as healing and [[Divination|divination]]. Ronald Hutton identified four definitions in use, ranging from anyone who contacts a spirit world in an altered state to the Indigenous religions of Siberia and neighboring parts of Asia.

Western anthropologists later applied the term broadly to unrelated practices in Asia, Africa, Australasia, and the Americas. Critics say this misapplies the words to the varied spiritual practices of [[Indigenous peoples]], each of which has its own terms. Studies report trance-related brain changes similar to those in meditation or hypnosis and psychological benefits such as reduced anxiety, but claims of literal contact with spirits lack verifiable evidence beyond subjective experience.

Domesticated ruminant mammal (*Ovis aries*) kept as [[Livestock|livestock]] for wool, meat, and milk. There were around 1.3 billion domestic sheep as of 2021. An adult female is a ewe, an intact male a ram, a castrated male a wether, and a young sheep a lamb. Sheep are [[Ruminant|ruminants]] and even-toed ungulates.

Sheep most likely descend from the wild mouflon of western Asia. They were among the earliest animals domesticated for agriculture, between about 9000 and 8500 BC in the region from the northern [[Zagros Mountains]] to southeastern [[Anatolia]]. By 4000 BC sheep reached from Britain to China. Selection for woolly sheep may have begun around 6000 BC, and the earliest woven wool garments date to around 4000 BC. In medieval England the [[Domesday Book]] records sheep outnumbering all other livestock combined. European colonists spread sheep to the New World from 1493 onward. Spain's prized [[Merino]] breed made it a major wool exporter, and Australia and New Zealand became major wool exporters in the 19th century. [[Carl Linnaeus]] named *Ovis aries* in the 1758 edition of *Systema Naturae*.

Sheep's wool is the most widely used animal fiber and is usually harvested by shearing. Lamb is meat from younger animals and mutton from older ones. Ewes range from 20–41 kg in the Soay to 77–113 kg in the Suffolk, and rams are typically 50 to 60 percent heavier than ewes. Sheep figure in many mythologies, such as the Golden Fleece, and in the Abrahamic religions, and are used as sacrificial animals. Australia, New Zealand, and the British Isles are most associated with sheep production, while China and India host among the largest flocks by count.

Chinese polymath, scientist, and statesman of the Northern [[Song dynasty]]. Born in Qiantang, modern [[Hangzhou]], he passed the imperial examinations and became a finance minister, state inspector, head of the Bureau of Astronomy, Assistant Minister of Imperial Hospitality, and academic chancellor. Politically he belonged to the Reformist New Policies Group led by Chancellor Wang Anshi. Political setbacks led to his retirement in 1085.

His main work, the *Dream Pool Essays* (*Mengxi Bitan*, 1088), made him the first to describe the magnetic needle [[Compass|compass]] used for navigation. He recognized true north through magnetic declination. In [[Astronomy|astronomy]] he improved the armillary sphere, gnomon, and sighting tube and invented a new type of inflow water clock. With his colleague Wei Pu he planned a five-year project of daily observations to map the orbits of the Moon and planets, which political opponents thwarted.

He proposed a hypothesis of land formation, an early account of [[Geomorphology|geomorphology]], based on inland marine [[Fossil|fossils]], soil erosion, and silt deposition. From petrified bamboos preserved underground in a dry northern region, he proposed gradual climate change. He was the first literary figure in China to mention the drydock. Though not the first to invent the [[Camera obscura|camera obscura]], he noted the relation between the focal point of a concave mirror and that of the pinhole. He wrote extensively on the movable type of Bi Sheng, and his writings preserved its legacy. An ancient crossbow mechanism he unearthed proved to be a Jacob's staff, a [[Surveying|surveying]] tool not known in Europe until 1321.

He also wrote on divination and the supernatural. Much of his other writing has not survived.
